concepts.title: Force as Push or Pull
concepts.definition: A force is a push or a pull that one body exerts on another; every force involves an interaction between two objects, is applied through contact or across a distance, and has both magnitude and direction.
concepts.key_idea: No force without an interaction: something pushes or pulls something else.
concepts.textbook_ref: hecu105.txt lines 43-130 (what is a force, interaction between two objects)

solution_steps.explain: Decide whether the body is pushed or pulled.
Name the two interacting objects; a force always needs both.
Both decide the final effect of the force.

concepts.title: What a Force Can Do to Objects
concepts.definition: A force can move a stationary object, stop a moving one, change its speed or direction of motion, and even change its shape - pressing, stretching or bending a body are all effects of force.
concepts.key_idea: Forces start, stop, redirect and deform - four signatures of a force at work.
concepts.textbook_ref: hecu105.txt lines 64-130 (what can a force do to objects)
question_patterns: list the effects a force can produce on an object

how does force change the direction of motion

solution_steps.explain: Forces may start motion, stop it, speed it up or slow it down.
A sideways force bends the path of a moving body.
Squeezing or stretching shows forces changing shape.

concepts.title: Types of Forces
concepts.definition: Forces come in families: muscular force acts through body contact, friction opposes sliding between surfaces in contact, while magnetic, electrostatic and gravitational forces act without touching, across empty space.
concepts.key_idea: Contact forces need touch; field forces such as gravity and magnetism act at a distance.
question_patterns: name the different types of forces with one example each
what is muscular force - is it a contact force
how does friction act on a sliding box
why do objects fall towards the earth - name the force
which forces act without contact between objects
classify magnetic, frictional and gravitational forces

solution_steps.explain: Muscular and frictional forces need touching surfaces.
Gravity, magnetism and static electricity pull or push across space.
Friction always opposes relative sliding between the surfaces.

concepts.title: Weight and Its Measurement
concepts.definition: Weight is the gravitational pull the earth exerts on a body; it is a force measured in newtons with a spring balance, whose stretch grows with the pull - readings like 1.6 N or 25.4 N state how strongly gravity acts on the object.
concepts.key_idea: Weight is a force in newtons, read from the stretch of a spring balance.
concepts.textbook_ref: hecu105.txt lines 456-681 (weight and its measurement, spring balance readings)
question_patterns: what is the difference between mass and weight
in which unit is weight measured and why
how does a spring balance measure weight

why is weight called a force
would your weight be the same on the moon - explain

solution_steps.explain: Weight is the earth's gravitational pull on the body, so its unit is the newton.
A spring balance stretches in proportion to the pull; the scale gives the reading in N.
Mass counts matter and stays the same everywhere; weight depends on gravity.

concepts.title: Floating and Sinking
concepts.definition: Whether an object floats or sinks in water is decided by the tug-of-war between its weight and the upward push of water on it; heavy-for-their-size objects sink while lighter ones float, and the comparison is judged through density.
concepts.key_idea: Float or sink is decided by comparing how much mass is packed per unit volume with water.
question_patterns: why does an iron nail sink while a ship floats
what decides whether an object floats or sinks in water
how does the upward push of water act on a submerged object
give two examples of floating and sinking from daily life
would an object that floats in water float in oil - reason
how can a heavy ship made of steel float

solution_steps.explain: Weight pulls down; water pushes up on the immersed object.
Objects less crowded with mass than water float; more crowded ones sink.
Ships spread their mass over a large volume, so their average crowdedness stays below water's.
